subtopic: REQUIREMENT THAT INJURIES TO CHILDREN BE REPORTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to call upon members of the medical profession to report to the attorneys general of their respective provinces within a week any bodily injuries to a child which may, in their opinion, have been caused by maltreatment. This move is prompted by the many cases which have been reported recently in newspapers. I believe this is a worthy amendment, and I do not believe any further dilation upon it at this time is necessary.

John S. Hodgson was born in Montreal, March 1, 1917, and educated at Montreal High School and McGill University. He was selected as a Rhodes scholar in 1937 and attended St. John's College, Oxford University. He was awarded his D. Phil, degree in economic history in 1940.
During 1940-41, Dr. Hodgson was in the Department of Labour where he worked on the drafting of the Unemployment Insurance Act. He served in the Canadian navy during the second world war 1941-45, for part of that time as assistant director of naval plans. He was awarded the O.B.E., and when demobilized held the rank of commander.
In 1946 Dr. Hodgson joined Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and in 1957 was appointed executive director. In 1959, he was appointed assistant secretary to the cabinet, a position he held until September 1, 1963, when he was appointed assistant deputy minister of national defence. He became principal secretary to the Prime Minister January 6, 1966.
From 1946-52, Dr. Hodgson was secretary of the Rhodes scholarship trust committee of the province of Quebec and in 1953 was its chairman. subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 5, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Sharp-Mr. Rinfret in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the decennial revision of the Bank Act and the extension of the charters of the existing chartered banks till July 1, 1976, and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) last night outlining the decennial revision of the Bank Act, I am pleased to support the attitude of the government which is giving the public a thorough reform of our financial system.
However, before discussing that resolution in detail, allow me to make a few comments on the reactions we have had about it so far. It is interesting to note that in the house last night the various spokesmen for the opposition parties adopted rather surprising and unrelated stands.
The Leader of the Opposition blamed the government for disregarding the proposal made by Mr. Justice Porter who recommended in 1964 the complete and immediate removal of the ceiling. He seemed to misunderstand the attitude of the Minister of Finance who said that in the present economic circumstances it is not possible to remove the ceiling immediately but that when the monetary situation has improved in the country, we will be able to remove it. Moreover, if he
Bank Act
had paid the slightest attention, he would have understood that the recommendation of the Porter Commission will eventually be implemented in our present system.
As far as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) is concerned, it is surprising to hear him say that he is not against the principle of removing the interest ceiling but that on the other hand, he is against the removal.
It is hard to understand that one can be in favour of a principle and against its application.
As far as the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) is concerned, he says that his business experience has led him to make numerous transactions with banks and that, although there is a ceiling on the interest rate, he has always paid more than 6 per cent, and he is asking the government to maintain what he himself considers useless, namely a ceiling rate of 6 per cent.
And, of course, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) agrees that more flexibility is needed in our system, that some loans at 6 per cent are not adequate and do not bring the banks enough, and I think that he shares the government's opinion on that matter.
I was pleased this morning to note that despite certain insinuations that we read in the newspapers, the president of the Royal Bank, Mr. McLaughlin, seemed very annoyed and dissatisfied with the present reforms. But, Mr. Chairman, we did not take action in the interest of banks, with all due deference to Mr. McLaughlin, but in the interest of the Canadian public.
This decennial revision will certainly be welcomed by the newspapers and the public as the most radical measure since the institution of the Bank of Canada about 30 years ago. It will likely increase the confidence of the public in our banking institutions and in any future decisions of the government concerning the monetary policy of our country.
Since the submission of the Porter report in February 1964, a great deal has been written and said on the reform of our finan-c al system, on the evils paralysing the efficiency of that system and on the possible cure. To sum up what the public in general pointed out, it is the absence of an actual and aggressive competition between the various financial institutions.
It is easy to note that the Minister of Finance has decided to implement the necessary reforms for such a competition between

July 6, 1966
Bank Act
all levels of financial institutions in Canada, and I think he should be very warmly commended.
Analysing the minister's statement, we realize immediately that the present banking reform deals with the very structure of our institutions and extends to their methods of dealing with the public.
Contrary to what the newspapers and commentators led us to believe recently, the minister's plan goes much beyond a simple change in the ceiling of interest rates. It grapples also with the very structure of the board of directors of banks, the qualifications of directors, and requires the disclosure of their reserve, of all kinds. It increases their field of action by allowing them to make mortgage loans; it sets up insurance for deposits and, moreover, it prohibits agreements between banks to fix interest rates.
The first point I should like to discuss, Mr. Chairman, is that of the ceiling on interest rates which has given rise in the last few weeks to much public curiosity. The Minister of Finance has just announced in his speech that the government intends to remove the present ceiling on the rate of interest charged by banks, when economic and monetary conditions in Canada are such that the decision of the government will not lead to unduly high rates of interest on bank loans.
The 6 per cent ceiling was adopted some 40 years ago, when the money market was entirely different from what it is now.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Indeed, at that time the rate of interest on bank loans or government loans was 1, 2 or 3 per cent, while the ceiling was 6 per cent. That ceiling gave a great deal of flexibility and elasticity to the banks, as there was a differential of at least 3 per cent between the normal rate on the market and the ceiling provided for by the act. That statutory ceiling has not been changed in 40 years. What was a ceiling then, is almost a floor now. Obviously, it is now an obstacle to normal money transactions; it has fostered the development of certain institutions which, using this lack of freedom for the banks, take an unfair advantage of such borrowers as have little credit, and occasionally charge them usurious rates of interest.
Under the present system, Mr. Chairman, big borrowers definitely have an edge over small people who need money. As banks have become the cheapest source of capital supply for corporate and individual borrowers, since there is a 6 per cent ceiling on interest rates,

there developed recently a practice which clearly discriminates against small borrowers.
Generally speaking, the small borrower who comes to a bank gets a loan at a rate higher than 6 per cent, since the banks have found a legal way to make personal loans at 9 and 10 per cent. This means that small borrowers, whom some people want to protect through a 6 per cent interest rate, enjoy no protection whatsoever in the present context.
It follows that the 6 per cent bank loan market is available to two particular types of borrowers, that is small businessmen and industrialists and big businessmen and industrialists.
As banks are limited to a 6 per cent ceiling, there is absolutely no leeway possible-

Mr. Chairman, as I was saying, banks are restricted to a 6 per cent ceiling and they are strictly prevented from speculating on the rate of interest when called upon to consider granting a loan to a particular person. Instead of diversifying their loans according to the risk involved and charge 6 per cent to some borrowers and 7 or 8 per cent to others, according to the risk, since they are not allowed any latitude at all, banks are forced to make loans at the best possible risks, at

Consequently, Mr. Chairman, there appears, between the small borrower and the banks, a useless middleman who increases considerably the cost of money. If the present ceiling on the interest rate were inexistent, the banks could possibly be in a position to lend to the small businessman or the small manufacturer with less security at a rate of 7 or 8 per cent. The banks would then be able to cover the additional risk and these people would not have to turn to finance companies.
The removal of the ceiling on the rate of interest, when financial conditions allow, will result in greater competition on the money market and banks will be able to compete with other financial institutions with regard to all sorts of loans. This competition will then diminish the rate of interest.
Bank, Act
The following is the best example of this fact. A few years ago, when only finance companies gave personal loans-for the banks had not found a legal way to do it-the rate of interest was much higher.
When banks began to deal with personal loans, competing with finance companies and other similar institutions, the rate of interest on personal loans fell to about 9, 10 and 11 per cent instead of the former 15, 16 and 17 per cent.
Thus we have seen, these last few years, the rate of interest on small loans become stabilized at around 10 per cent. Therefore, if the present reform allows banks to deal with all types of loans, including mortgage loans, this additional competition on the Canadian loan market will lower the rate of interest, for there will be greater competition to attract borrowers, and I think everyone will profit thereby.

Mr. Chairman, let me call your attention to a case which struck me tremendously and shows very clearly the existing gap in our system.
Some large companies and municipal corporations misuse the system in this way: as bank interest rates for company loans to the corporations cannot exceed 6 per cent, some big borrowers request short-term bank loans at this rate under the usual pretences.
For instance, a company intended some time ago to go on the security market to finance an undertaking of $5 million. Those people went to a banker and explained their problem. They said: We will go on the security market in three months to borrow $5

July 6, 1966
Bank Act
million; since we urgently need funds, could you lend us immediately $5 million at 6 per cent for three months?
Of course, the bank which is an institution to finance large companies on a short-term and long-term basis agreed to lend them $5 million at 6 per cent. When the three-month period expired, the banker asked that company to reimburse the $5 million. The company which, three months before, has given the banker a letter saying that it intended to go on the market in the following weeks told him: Unfortunately, we are not in a position to pay you back, we are no longer interested in going on the market, because if we do we will not pay 6 per cent but 6J per cent.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
And so, instead of giving a temporary loan of $5 million for three months, the bank had to extend the term of the loan over a period of months and even years. Consequently, it did not have that $5 million to loan small borrowers. Moreover, there was no way for it to force the company to borrow on the market. Naturally, this unbalance was due to the fact that banks are not supposed to finance long term projects; they are intended to provide short term loans to those companies.
The net result is that the banks' important source of short term funds is exhausted for the benefit of large companies; the small borrower, the small merchant and the small industrialist must turn to the near-banks, to which the ceiling does not apply, to borrow money at interest rates of 12, 14 and 15 per cent instead of borrowing from banks for perhaps 7 or 8 per cent, depending on their ability to reimburse and their credit rate.
May I be permitted, on this score, to quote from an editorial published in the newspaper Le Devoir for Tuesday, June 28, 1966 over the signature of Mr. Claude Ryan:
If the banks are to play a dynamic role within our financial system, for what reason should they be bound by limits which, if they were strictly observed, would reduce them to marginal factors in the system. In fact, the current situation breaks down the borrowers into two classes: the safe borrowers (generally the large borrowers) who are the primary beneficiaries of the 6 per cent loan system and the others-the small businessmen, the small manufacturers, the thousands upon thousands of individuals-who are being blindly cast into the maws of the 10 per cent and over lenders. Paradoxically, those who favour higher interest rates are running the risk of being considered as big, bad wolves while, in fact, the puritanical maintenance of the prevailing dichotomic situation seems much more contrary to the real benefit of the public.

I could also quote another editorial from a newspaper which is the mouthpiece of small businessmen, asking for the removal of this ceiling, which is unfavourable to the small businessmen.

We have said before in these columns that small business is often too big a risk at the rate of six per cent interest for the bank to touch him. We have often said that the ceiling should either be raised or removed altogether to make small business more attractive to the banks.

And this newspaper is the official mouthpiece of small businessmen in Ontario.
Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I think it is only fair to say it is of the utmost importance for us to take the necessary steps in order to rectify the situation as concerns our banking system, namely: to play an energetic and positive part in our economy and, to this end, our banks must, by all means, compete with one another, so as to secure the best rate and service possible for consumers. At present, there is no competition at all between banks, since they have no freedom at all, and with such a system, instead of providing loans under some kind of competition, they are using discretion that often promotes only the interests of the friends of the system and the people close to our major banking institutions.
On this point, I am happy to see that the Minister of Finance mentioned in his speech that he would take the necessary steps to prevent banks from agreeing among themselves to set a rate of interest to be paid on deposits and a rate of interest they would charge on the loans they make. The rate should be fixed by competition, and that is how we will see real competition between all our financial institutions. That will be greatly helped if this liberalization of the Canada Bank Act promotes the establishment of new banks in Canada.
I am also happy to see that the house passed yesterday the bill establishing the Bank of Western Canada. I am glad the minister mentioned in his speech yesterday that the government wishes to see many new banks established, so as to promote competition between these vital institutions in our system.
As the hon. member for Lapointe is familiar with the banking system, he may try to have a bank of his own.

This is where we have some difference of opinion, in relation to these certain changes in connection with the administration of the act. As we all know, I am sure, the banking system in Canada has given excellent service to the people of this country. I think Canadian citizens have a feeling of security which not all the citizens of other countries have. We have considered the banks to be a bulwark, and in this connection we must pay credit to the Inspector General of Banks, who for many years has had the policing job to do. I believe he has done it energetically and efficiently. It must be remembered that while the banks are in business to make money, and I have no quarrel whatever with that objective, I do feel, however, that they should be considered as a rather select group of corporations which have an obligation to serve the Canadian people. Our job as members of parliament is to see that Canadians are served to the best of their interests by the banks.
I do not think that the citizens of Canada, Mr. Chairman, are being so served by this government in its present amendments to the act. This government has not met the threat of inflation or the rising cost of living and is not doing anything to meet those situations now. I have in mind the interests of the small businessman, the farmer and the small borrower. These people are not going to receive any benefit from the proposed amendments to the Bank Act. I have heard and read that the tight money which we now have is probably going to get tighter. This cannot be allowed to happen. But this government, Mr. Chairman, is obviously accepting the situation and doing nothing about it.
The minister last evening outlined in general terms what he referred to as certain proposed amendments to the Bank Act. I cannot help but emphasize that they were certainly in very general terms. Of course, .the one main item of the whole group of amendments that is of interest to all of the Canadian people is the interest rate amendment. The present ceiling on interest is 6 per cent, but in this respect we are really very little wiser than when the minister began his comments. The minister suggested that it should be tied to the average market yield on short-term government bonds. I am assuming that there will be some fixed percentage over and above the average yield but at the moment, of course, we do not know. We are told that we will find out.

The minister also suggested last evening that when this bill goes to the finance, trade and economic affairs committee for study it would be a good idea to examine this formula very closely to see whether it is the best alternative. I can assure him, Mr. Chairman, that that examination will be given.
However, let me repeat that we are still in the dark as to just what the interest rate is going to be and how it will operate. I suppose that a floating rate of this nature, as you might call it, might have some merit in the case of very credit-worthy risks, but I do not see how this can be of any assistance, as I said earlier, to the small businessman, the farmer or the small borrower. They are the ones who are going to suffer. They are the ones who will be forced to go to other money lenders and will have to pay much higher interest rates.
While there may be some connection between the rate on government bonds and the general requirements of the economy, there are other features affecting the price of government bonds, such as stock market prices, whichever stock happens to be the more attractive, the United States money market situation, deficit or surplus financing of the Canadian economy, balancing of international payments and so on. They may or may not be consistent with the needs of the economy and of business but, sir, all these factors are going to affect the interest rate for business borrowers. It is like trying to find the correct price of bananas by analysing the demand for and supply of fish eggs, or you can use any other comparison. It is going to be just about as difficult as that.
On the whole, as far as these amendments go I claim that the Porter Commission report might just as well have been forgotten. The commission might just as well have not met. The minister could have produced the amendments which he has put before us and has outlined in such a vague way without any report at all.
I should like to refer to the two main recommendations made in the Porter Commission report, and I think they go hand in hand. One was to the effect that the near banks should be brought under federal control. The other was the removal of the interest ceiling. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that these two go together hand in hand.
If such a procedure had been adopted, then I think it would be fair to all concerned. As it is, we are not getting competition. The near banks are going to be left to operate on their

should be remedied. There are different opinions about the Bank Act, and I think the legality of the question I have raised should be straightened out.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been evidence in the speeches on the opposition side, both this afternoon and last evening, of some dissatisfaction with the statement that the minister made on the basis that it did not provide sufficient information for the opposition to deal with this matter. Notwithstanding that complaint, the opposition nevertheless has been able to make statements of far reaching consequence which would seem to contradict their earlier statements. I think it is consistent, however, with the procedure at this stage of debate that this matter should follow the course that has been followed with regard to resolutions. There is nothing inconsistent in relation to the practice of this chamber in debating the resolution stage of a bill. Therefore I do not think that the complaints stand on any solid foundation.
One of the responsibilities, it seems to me, of government and parliament in this matter is to look at the effectiveness of our existing financial policy in order to determine ways and means of strengthening that policy so that it may better serve the requirements of our economy. In this discussion we must be concerned about the adequacy of our financial system to meet the needs of our society in an efficient and creative way. We must have a properly functioning financial system which will serve the needs of the greatest possible number of people.
In attempting to achieve this laudable goal we ought to take into consideration the past record and effectiveness of our financial policies and financial system. We must have as far as possible a reasonable understanding of the changes which have taken place in our economy, and we must also consider wider problems which confront our economy so that we may be better able to understand the role that financial policies may be expected to play in the country's development.

If a financial system is not adequately fulfilling its functions, or is fulfilling them in an improper or imperfect way, the result will surely be an adverse effect on the economy. I would therefore suggest once again that providing as much flexibility and as much scope as possible to meet the demands for highly developed borrowing facilities which are part of any complex economy is something that is necessary.
One of the main requisites of a financial system in the present day and in the future Canada is a high degree of flexibility. One of the most frequent criticisms of the present system and the present policies has to do with the lack of flexibility and the desirable degree of competition to meet adequately the present needs of our economy.
This criticism comes from many quarters. We have heard it in the house before and in the debate so far. There are suggestions that our present system discriminates against certain classes of borrowers and savers and-this is of particular interest to me-against certain regions because it does not provide services to all. In some instances the services provided are of an inadequate nature. It seems that our criticism perhaps is aimed directly at the financial institutions, because these are the vehicles for transmitting financial policy.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The challenge before the government in introducing this legislation is to bring forward a measure which will have the effect of increasing competition and flexibility in our banking system. I was pleased, therefore, with the references made to this subject in the minister's speech. At this point in the debate it is reasonable to assume we are talking in terms of principles and not in detail. Opposition speakers have expressed an interest in detail but, as they well know, this is not in keeping with our procedure at this stage.
If this country is to develop its economic potential to the maximum it has to afford to all of its people the greatest possible opportunities to participate in our economic development and one of the essentials of such a plan for progress is a creative financial system, one which is not just passive but innovating and capable of meeting changed circumstances with new ideas and new approaches.
As I have indicated, my particular concern is the role of financial policy and of our financial institutions in those regions of Canada which have not yet achieved the
July 6, 1966

Bank Act
degree of development reached by some of our more fortunate areas. In many other fields the government, in fact, successive governments, have introduced policies aimed at developing these less-developed parts of Canada. We are all aware of the activities of the Atlantic Development Board, the Area Development Agency and similar agencies. But we shall only achieve the desired goals in this sphere if our financial system also plays its full part in the development of equal opportunities in all areas of Canada. At the present time our system lacks both the flexibility and the element of competition which are so badly needed and the absence of which has had a particularly adverse effect on those regions of Canada which are removed from the centre.
Since the thirties, when banks in the United States failed, we have continued to believe something which is in many ways a myth, namely, that the Canadian banking system is vastly superior to that of the United States. However, I suggest there are many features of the United States banking system which are attractive, particularly to those of us who do not come from the central regions of Canada. We have, in a sense, suffered because of the branch banking system, and any efforts which can be made to assist the growth of regional banks and to create more flexibility and competition in the system would surely be of benefit to us.
Naturally we hear protestations from bankers in this country that there is no such thing as discrimination, that all areas are treated alike. Undoubtedly this is a subject which will be discussed at considerable length when this bill goes before the committee. But while there may be evidence to suggest that in the province of Nova Scotia, for example, the amount of money lent is related to the amount collected by the banks in that province in the form of savings, I nevertheless feel there is a rigidity which has a particularly adverse effect on regions far removed from the centre.
There are other details which were mentioned by the minister and which will have the effect of helping to create an environment for more flexibility and competition. Hon. members opposite have directed their remarks to the question of deposit insurance. I believe this is a good measure. It will certainly make the establishment of new banks easier. I also believe it will strengthen nearbanks and make them more creditable institutions.
One result of this legislation will be a provision under which banks will find it necessary to declare their inner reserves. This is important because there is always a certain amount of mythology surrounding banks and the banking system, and close to 100 per cent of it is pure mythology. Many of the attitudes adopted by bankers and others in the system who tend to be over-cautious are interwoven with the mythology which surrounds our banking institutions. I welcome this move to have inner reserves made public and to provide for a system of deposit insurance.
There has been some discussion about the recommendations of the Porter Commission concerning near-banks. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Perth, if I remember correctly, was critical of the Minister of Finance for not dealing with this subject. However, no less an authority than the distinguished member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands spoke of the constitutional difficulties in this field. Both hon. members were unsatisfied, but I believe the intention of the minister to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss the broad theme of consumer credit represents a most important step toward resolving the whole question of the relationship between near-banks and banks.

I suggest there is a relationship and that this conference will be a meaningful one. More important still, I believe the government ought at the earliest opportunity to give detailed study to ways and means of surmounting the constitutional difficulties which, according to some hon. members, prevent our bringing the near-banks under the control of the Bank Act. The relationship which I see between this and the forthcoming federal-provincial conference is that we shall be discussing with the provinces the whole question of consumer credit. I do not believe any province would have a strong case for wishing to prevent provincial institutions being subjected to uniform regulation and control, since this control would be of benefit to borrowers. It would certainly be of particular benefit to small borrowers, and I doubt that

July 6, 1966
Bank Act
any provincial government would wish openly to oppose a course of action beneficial to this group.
The approach taken by the minister in introducing this legislation suggests he is well aware of the need for flexibility and competition, that he is aware of the problem presented by the near-banks, and that these important questions, which are matters of concern to members on all sides, will receive greater attention from the present Minister of Finance than they have had for some time.
There has to be a philosophy behind our approach to financial policy. Our philosophy, it would seem, is to afford as far as possible an equal break for all who are dealing with the system, whether it is a small borrower or a particular region of the country which now suffers certain disadvantages. Notwithstanding the advantages of confederation there are still certain disadvantages suffered by regions removed from the centre. I believe it is within the ambit of this philosophy that the present administration is approaching this measure for the revision of the Bank Act.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
An important factor is the attitude of those in financial institutions. I have never been particularly cognizant of any progressive or enlightened attitude on the part of many of them. They seem to have a standard routine of rejecting anything that suggests government control or government interference. In many ways our financial institutions are the last preserve of the old laissez-faire attitude in our economy.
I am sure many hon. members would agree that notwithstanding the changes in economic attitudes during the last 30 years one thing has remained consistent, that no matter what attempts have been made to increase opportunities in Canada and no matter what success we have had in giving more people more wealth, those at the top of the system always seem to do well. There should be a greater awareness on the part of financial institutions of what we are trying to do in the economic development of Canada. They ought not to be restricted by prejudice or preconceived notions regarding the role of government. Such a change of attitude is very necessary because these institutions are not very popular. They do not really belong to the community.
This is particularly correct if, as those of us on the outer fringes have to do, one deals with branches of the various banks. They are impersonal and because of their operation

they are to a large degree divorced from the needs of the people. Notwithstanding the merits of the branch banking system this factor is of considerable importance, but it is one that can be rectified by a greater awareness on the part of the financial institutions of the role that they must play in our economic development.
For example, from time to time in the field of monetary policy we are confronted with philosophical decisions regarding the flow of credit. Such a philosophical decision is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada, but once it is made on the basis of what is good for Canada as a whole its application is left up to the individuals in the various financial institutions. This is a great weakness because in the first instance it is generally due to inflationary pressures that a course of action is taken. But I suggest these inflationary pressures are not universal and therefore in my view our monetary policy ought to reflect more the regional differences that exist in this country. If this is not being done by regulation, then it seems to me those within the system have a responsibility to bear these factors in mind in their own administration.
Individuals in the system with whom I have discussed the matter have told me that at no time would they discriminate against any group or individual. My reply was that this is exactly the point, that there are groups who, because of lack of opportunity or lack of development, need special concern and there are other special factors to be taken into consideration, so that some kind of philosophy in this regard should be more in evidence in our financial institutions.
It may be said that this is not good economics, the only criterion being the return in a monetary sense, but I challenge that because I do not believe it is a sophisticated view in Canada today in that other value judgments are made. This was the basis of the laissez-faire attitude, that what was best in terms of dollars was best in terms of people, but it is many years since we discovered that this is not true. The relationship of our financial policies to our development policies should be emphasized more.
By expressing his recognition of the need for flexibility in competition the minister has gone farther than any of his predecessors in meeting this problem and in suggesting what is going to be in the bill and, like other hon. members, I look forward to seeing the bill so that it may receive the kind of in depth study that is not and should not be possible at this stage of the proceedings.
July 6. 1966

Before resuming my seat I wish to mention one other matter which may not be completely relevant, namely, the relationship of the Industrial Development Bank to the Bank of Canada. The minister ought to give serious consideration to that relationship and to the greater use that may be made of the Industrial Development Bank in assisting the development of various regions. I know there will be objections raised to this by the financial institutions themselves, but perhaps some of them might pick up their socks and fill some of the void.
I would like again to congratulate the minister for introducing this measure which he has described as a blueprint for competition. Lack of competition has been one of the big weaknesses in our system. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has pointed out some of the difficulties to be overcome in introducing competition within the system, but I think the minister has outlined the most positive approach we have ever had to this vital problem.

Mr. Chairman, the discussion of a resolution preceding extensive revision of the Bank Act should involve some consideration of the general principles governing our approach to banking legislation in Canada. I regret that the minister did not devote somewhat more attention in his speech to the question of the general principles which he feels should be embodied in the revision, if only for the purpose that when we get the bill we can test the details of the legislation against the principles which it might be agreed should be served by that legislation and reflected in it.
Not having the advantage of any statement in detail by the government as to its views in this regard, nevertheless I feel it is important a statement should be made, and with some trepidation I would like to outline what I feel are some of the general principles which we should now wish to see incorporated in a revision of the Bank Act, looking forward to the future and to the enabling of the financial and monetary system of this country to meet the problems of today and of years to come.
I would say that the first general principle is the maintenance and, when necessary, the extension of effective jurisdiction over the banking system, something which is essential to any government which claims effective control of monetary policy or, indeed, monetary and fiscal policy. If we do not have that effective control of the banking system, then
Bank Act
to say we intend to exercise control over monetary policy is a mere pretence.
A second and corollary principle is that a strong and effective banking system-and the word "effective" here includes the qualities of flexibility and competitiveness-is the indispensable right arm of government in the exercise of that effective control over the monetary system.
Third, parliament and government must therefore be concerned to maintain the integrity of the banking system, and by this I mean not just the strength of existing banks but the integrity and viability of the entire system, as well as the integrity of their control over that system.
Fourth, parliament and government must be concerned not only to maintain the soundness and effectiveness of the institutions within the banking system as presently officially constituted, but must assert and extend control over any other institutions or trends which, if left unchecked, would erode the strength of and the control over that system.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Fifth, in approaching our responsibilities in these connections we must remember that our concern is not just for the strength and well-being of the system and its institutions in isolation but also for the establishment and extension of a system and institutions which will serve the needs of the economy as a whole and the interests of depositors and borrowers individually. We must therefore always be concerned, in legislation and regulation of the institutions, to reconcile the two cardinal requirements of safety or strength on the one hand, and effectiveness or competition on the other.
I must say as a personal opinion, from looking at the present situation in the Canadian banking system and the institutions which officially constitute it at the moment, that in our system and in the legislation for the future we could safely place considerably more emphasis on flexibility and competitiveness both in the interest of the financial community and of the public. I regret that in my view the outline of the legislation given by the minister does not go far enough in that direction.
The legislation which we are to examine, and which will be based on this resolution, in my view should reflect at least those principles-and I have only summarized some which are applicable. I do not think anyone would

disagree that the Porter Commission's approach certainly reflected those principles. I would have hoped that the legislation would reflect more faithfully not only those principles but also the approach and recommendations of the Porter Commission. In my view it falls very considerably short of that desired objective and falls short especially in connection with control in the interest of small businesses and small borrowers.
When I use the word "small" here I do not mean in matters of loans of, say, $1,000, because in terms of the size of Canadian business today I think we have to realize that even $100,000 in relation to what is going on in the financial institutions of Canada is relatively, and I am speaking relatively only, a small business or small borrower. Although $100,000 dollars seems a great deal of money to me, yet in terms of the size and sophistication of the Canadian financial system I think anything up to $100,000 probably should be classified in the field of the smaller business and smaller borrower.
As I said, I regret that the legislation does not reflect the recommendations and the approach of the Porter Commission, anything like as completely as I would like to see it do. In considering the extent to which we would like to see the recommendations of the Porter Commission followed it is helpful to examine some of the authoritative statements which have been made about that commission and its work. I should like to refer the committee to an article that appeared in The Canadian Banker in the summer of 1964, by Professor Slater, a professor of economics at Queen's University. Not all of what he said was uniformly flattering. However, at pages 8 and 9 he gives his assessment of the work of the commission as a whole. I think these passages are of very great significance. He said:
The independence, honesty and frankness of the report are particularly noteworthy. This commission has struggled hard to avoid being in anybody's pocket.
In other words, the recommendations made are not just in the interests of the banks as such but are in the interests of the economy as a whole. He went on:
Each set of ideas coming before the commission has been examined carefully, confronted with the tests of logic and experience and put into relationship with other ideas and evidence.
Again, he said:
For the most part the report is competent and judicious. The analysis in some sections is markedly superior to that in the comparable British and American documents. Nearly every issue of banking and financial policy is examined; the pros and

cons are given at least a quick and rough weighing, and at most a careful and balanced evaluation. In my judgment the report will be immediately helpful in the review of Canadian banking and financial legislation, and in the formulation and exercise of financial and related general economic policy.
He said further:
In my view, one of the most attractive features of the report is its neutrality and cleanness with respect to the social and political climate. The commissioners are firm that economic affairs are subsidiary to political and social choices. The effect of many of their recommendations is to facilitate the responsible exercise of government power.
Finally:
In a general appreciation of the report, the comprehensiveness of the work also deserves comment. The commission has taken on nearly every major issue of financial performance or policy which has concerned people during the last two decades. A special effort has been made to use effectively the best of the modern theoretical and empirical studies of money and finance.
Mr. Chairman, that being an impartial assessment of the merits of the Porter Commission's studies and recommendations, it is interesting to turn to the brief statement of objectives which the commission itself sought to achieve in the recommendations it brought down. These are the broad economic objectives which Canada should attain and which the commission felt would be facilitated by its recommendations. They are stated as follows in the report at page 398:
(a)	Rising productivity;
(b)	A high and stable level of employment;
(c)	Stable prices;
(d)	A sound external financial position.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to conceive of a better statement of financial and economic objectives for Canada. Therefore it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that, to the extent that the recommendations of the Porter commission would bring about these objectives, it is regrettable in the extreme that those recommendations are not followed. 1 have said that I think the outline of the legislation given by the minister indicates several important areas in which they are not followed. I should like to refer to them briefly at this stage.
The first omission is that the Porter commission recommended that near-banks and similar institutions should come under the same umbrella by way of banking legislation as the present banking institutions themselves so that they would all be made competitive with a view to avoiding, as they clearly point out, the situation in which certain borrowers are
July 6. 1966

compelled to go where they must pay 14 per cent, 16 per cent, 18 per cent and up to 24 per cent on their money with disastrous effect. The only result of such excessive rates is inflation in respect of the cost of goods and services that are produced and purchased by Canadians. The Porter Commission wanted all these institutions made competitive under the one legislative umbrella.
In the legislation outlined by the minister the only approach in this regard is to introduce the device of deposit insurance. I think there will be general agreement that deposit insurance is a good and desirable development so far as it goes, but in respect of this particular problem may I suggest it is of dubious value so far as dealing with the whole area is concerned because there are so many gaps and so many parts of the problem which will not be tackled effectively by the device of deposit insurance.

I am not one to minimize the constitutional problems and the difficulties that sometimes confront us in relations between governments. But I think this matter should be discussed with the provinces on a co-operative basis, and without denying the right of the provinces to incorporate these companies and to lay down regulations which must be complied with within the province, it could be pointed out that because many of these institutions do business outside the province a degree of co-operation within the ambit of federal legislation is desirable and is in the interests of the protection of depositors, borrowers and the economy generally. I think it would be difficult, if proprly approached, for responsible provincial governments to refuse at least to discuss the problem and approach it along these lines. Such a solution would be in keeping with the Porter Commission recommendations.
The importance of this matter can be understood by recalling the appalling situation brought about by the collapse of Atlantic

July 6, 1966
Bank Act
Acceptance Corporation just last year, a collapse of which we are still feeling the effects with respect to the availability of credit in th Canadian economy. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister and the committee, that it is doubtful whether the Canadian financial system could stand another such collapse. Certainly confidence in the system would be totally destroyed in so far as overseas money is concerned, investors from outside Canada, and I doubt whether even the system within Canada could stand another such collapse.
Therefore any approach along the lines recommended by the Porter Commission to place these and related types of institutions under the umbrella of the federal banking laws would be most desirable, and it is regrettable that the minister does not indicate a greater determination in pursuing such a solution to this part of the problem.
Next, the Porter Commission recommended that lending companies and lending charges -here I am thinking of the small loan companies-be also regulated in the same way and placed under the banking legislation. I refer, Mr. Chairman, to the recommendation found at page 382 of the commission report, which reads:
At present the small loan companies and licensed moneylenders are regulated by the Superintendent of Insurance under the Small Loans Act, which sets limits on the charges they may levy for cash loans. As noted in the previous chapter, we believe that all cash lenders-including the banking institutions-should be subject to uniform regulation, and we think it appropriate that supervision of the amended legislation be transferred to the Inspector General of Banks.
I regret that this step does not appear to be forecast as one of the features of the legislation to be introduced.
Third, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the legislation, in the outline given by the minister, repeats the damaging and dangerous position taken by his predecessor; that is to say, there will be a feature in the legislation involving the punishment of a certain bank by way of retroactive legislation, a bank incorporated under laws as they existed at one time and placed in an invidious and very inferior position as a result of a change in the laws introduced after it had properly applied for and received its incorporation. It is, further more, a situation brought about by means of a device which if resorted to elsewhere would very seriously and adversely affect the branches and agencies of Canadian banks operating outside Canada.

In addition to these objections to the provisions of the legislation I wish to raise certain other considerations in connection with the legislation about which I feel very strongly. I am thinking of the whole course followed with respect to this legislation, the delays, uncertainties and the consequent adverse effect these have had upon the plans and operations of the Canadian financial community. After all, the Porter Commission report was brought down in 1964. The decennial Bank Act revision was due in 1964. The introduction of the legislation has been held up by quarrels, delays and uncertainty within the Liberal cabinet ever since. The legislation is now two years overdue and, as is well known without my rehearsing the detail, plans have recently had to be revised substantially as a result of further very serious disagreements within the ranks of the government.

We will not be able to have the debate on second reading until we come back, and we do not know when we are coming back nor does the financial community. My experience and that of others is that the debate on second reading and the study in committee of this legislation will occupy two to three months, and one assumes, on the basis of past experience again, that there will be a prorogation of this session toward the end of the year. Where does that leave the minister, the legislation, the banking system and the financial institutions of Canada? Will we have to start all over again in another session of parliament? I only point out these things to emphasize the serious position in which the delay and inability of the government to get on with this legislation have placed our economy.
July 6, 1966

The final point I want to make is with respect to the matter of the central feature of the Porter Commission's recommendations and one of the essential features of the bill, namely, the question of the interest ceiling. What are we told? We were told by the minister last night that at some time in the future the interest ceiling on bank loans will be lifted but that in the meantime a formula will be provided for a flexible interest ceiling related to the yield of short-term government bonds. This leaves us with tremendously important questions as to the principle of the legislation, questions to which we were denied answers last night and still are denied them. First, with regard to when the ceiling would be lifted the minister slid over this question in his speech. He said, as reported at page 7236 of Hansard:
Naturally, no one can say just when general interest rates will decline to the point that will release the ceiling on bank interest rates. I would hope it would come sooner rather than later, so that the proper development and evolution of our financial system as a whole can proceed on the basis of effective competition.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
But we were given no indication as to when it will come. The question remains: will the point of time at which the changeable formula and the ceiling are removed, be determined or fixed by the legislation or by some device embodied in the legislation or will it be fixed at the whim of the executive? This is a tremendously important matter of principle, that the control of banking legislation reside in parliament and that fundamental changes in the banking legislation not be made without reference to parliament. I submit that most certainly the question of a change in the method of fixing the interest ceiling, or indeed the question of the removal of the interest ceiling-the movement from one stage to another-is a most important and fundamental matter which should not be decided without reference to parliament. And yet we are not told how this is dealt with in the legislation. This is the kind of information which we sought last night and which unfortunately we have been denied up to this point.
And so I say, together with my colleague, the hon. member for Perth, that we are not prepared to support this resolution because of the serious omissions from the legislation as outlined by the minister, and because of the objections to the way in which it has been introduced and the lack of information on it. While maintaining a flexibility of decision
Bank Act
with respect to the legislation when we see it, we are not prepared to support at present a resolution which seems to us to beg many of the fundamental questions which should be faced and dealt with in the revision of the Bank Act.
When the legislation itself comes in, we will measure it against the principles I have outlined and the recommendations of the Porter report, and to the extent it conforms to them we will support it; to the extent it does not conform to them, we will oppose it.

The Canada Pension Plan is a long-range program. One of the objectives of the Canada Assistance Plan is to meet the needs of those people now retired who will draw no Canada Pension Plan benefits and those who will retire in the next ten years and will be unable to build up full retirement pensions during the transitional period.

of many younger people engaged in primary industries in marginal communities. At the same time, a $100 pension would not meet all the needs of aged persons living in the higher-cost urban centres.

Increased federal expenditures for old age security would have an effect on the over-all priorities for other federal expenditures.
